On the 1938 map, Algeria (France) is French Algeria stretching deep into the Sahara, a century after the conquest that began in 1830.

In 1930 France held grand celebrations for the hundredth year of its rule. The north was legally part of France, divided into three departments, and around a million European settlers lived there. The Muslim majority, some six million, mostly could not vote for the French parliament. A 1936 plan to give citizenship to a small Muslim elite, the Blum and Viollette bill, never even reached a vote after settler protests.

This was the decade when Algerian nationalism took shape:

  • Messali Hadj led the North African Star and, from 1937, the Algerian People's Party, calling for independence.
  • The cleric Abdelhamid Ben Badis founded the Association of Muslim Ulema in 1931, teaching that Algeria was Arab and Muslim, not French.

After the Sétif and Guelma massacres of 1945 the gap grew into the Algerian War. For the earlier colony, see French Algeria in 1880; for the free state, Algeria.
